lessons.name: Analyze passages from To Kill a Mockingbird : Part 1

content.text: Read the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, Scout Finch, the narrator, is starting the first grade.

textContent.text: Miss Caroline began the day by reading us a story about cats. The cats had long conversations with one another, they wore cunning little clothes and lived in a warm house beneath a kitchen stove. By the time Mrs. Cat called the drugstore for an order of chocolate malted mice the class was wriggling like a bucketful of catawba worms. Miss Caroline seemed unaware that the ragged, denim-shirted and floursack-skirted first grade, most of whom had chopped cotton and fed hogs from the time they were able to walk, were immune to imaginative literature. Miss Caroline came to the end of the story and said, "Oh, my, wasn't that nice?"
Then she went to the blackboard and printed the alphabet in enormous square capitals, turned to the class and asked, "Does anybody know what these are?"
Everybody did; most of the first grade had failed it last year.

I suppose she chose me because she knew my name; as I read the alphabet a faint line appeared between her eyebrows, and after making me read most of My First Reader and the stock-market quotations from The Mobile Register aloud, she discovered that I was literate and looked at me with more than faint distaste. Miss Caroline told me to tell my father not to teach me any more, it would interfere with my reading.

"Teach me?" I said in surprise. "He hasn't taught me anything, Miss Caroline. Atticus ain't got time to teach me anything," I added, when Miss Caroline smiled and shook her head. "Why, he's so tired at night he just sits in the living room and reads."

"If he didn't teach you, who did?" Miss Caroline asked good-naturedly. "Somebody did. You weren't born reading The Mobile Register […] Now you tell your father not to teach you any more. It's best to begin reading with a fresh mind. You tell him I'll take over from here and try to undo the damage—"
"Ma'am?"
"Your father does not know how to teach. You can have a seat now."

I mumbled that I was sorry and retired meditating upon my crime. I never deliberately learned to read, but somehow I had been wallowing illicitly in the daily papers. In the long hours of church—was it then I learned? I could not remember not being able to read hymns. Now that I was compelled to think about it, reading was something that just came to me, as learning to fasten the seat of my union suit without looking around, or achieving two bows from a snarl of shoelaces. I could not remember when the lines above Atticus's moving finger separated into words, but I had stared at them all the evenings in my memory, listening to the news of the day, Bills To Be Enacted into Laws, the diaries of Lorenzo Dow—anything Atticus happened to be reading when I crawled into his lap every night. Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird
tells the story of Scout Finch, a young girl growing up in a small town in Alabama in the 1930s, during a period of widespread racial segregation in the United States.

pieces.text: At the beginning of the novel, Scout and her brother, Jem, keep themselves busy by plotting to uncover the mysteries of their reclusive neighbor, Mr. Arthur "Boo" Radley. But when their father, well-respected lawyer Atticus Finch, sparks controversy by agreeing to defend an African American man in an upcoming trial, Scout's world turns upside-down.

content.text: Scout and her family are forced to reckon with the hate and racial prejudice embedded in their community.

pieces.text: When it was first published in 1960,

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: resonated with countless readers experiencing the turmoil of the Civil Rights Movement in the United States. The novel is famous for the way it uses the innocent perspective of a child to illuminate the brutal realities of racism in the United States during that period of American history.

contents.text: The details in this passage suggest that this is the most likely reason why Scout apologizes to Miss Caroline:

text.text: She realizes that she has displeased her teacher, even if she doesn't comprehend why her actions were wrong.

content.text: Scout notes that Miss Caroline looks at her "with more than faint distaste," so she understands that she has displeased her teacher. But after apologizing, Scout puzzles over her "crime" and tries to figure out where she went wrong.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not suggest that these are reasons why Scout apologizes:

text.text: She regrets embarrassing her teacher by making it look like Miss Caroline's teaching efforts are ineffective.

content.text: Scout's narration does not suggest that Miss Caroline is embarrassed, so it is unlikely that this is Scout's concern.

text.text: She now understands that being taught to read a certain way at home will inhibit her classroom education.

content.text: Though Miss Caroline asserts that Scout's education has been damaged by her father's teaching, Scout insists that her father has not been teaching her how to read at home. So, it is unlikely that she now understands or shares Miss Caroline's sentiments regarding reading.

text.text: She is apologizing sarcastically because she knows she has not actually done anything wrong.

content.text: Scout mumbles her apology instead of pointedly or loudly responding to the teacher, so her behavior does not suggest sarcasm or defiance.

content.text: Read the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, Scout Finch (the narrator), Jem (her brother), and Dill (a friend) attempt to deliver a note to Mr. Arthur "Boo" Radley, their mysterious and reclusive neighbor, before they are caught by Atticus (Scout and Jem's father).

textContent.text: [Jem] scuttled beneath the house and came out with a yellow bamboo pole. "Reckon this is long enough to reach from the sidewalk?"
"Anybody who's brave enough to go up and touch the house hadn't oughta use a fishin' pole," I said. "Why don't you just knock the front door down?"
"This—is—different," said Jem, "how many times do I have to tell you that?"

Jem attached the note to the end of the fishing pole, let the pole out across the yard and pushed it toward the window he had selected. The pole lacked several inches of being long enough, and Jem leaned over as far as he could. I watched him making jabbing motions for so long, I abandoned my post and went to him.
"Can't get it off the pole," he muttered, "or if I get it off I can't make it stay. G'on back down the street, Scout."

I returned and gazed around the curve at the empty road. Occasionally I looked back at Jem, who was patiently trying to place the note on the window sill. It would flutter to the ground and Jem would jab it up, until I thought if Boo Radley ever received it he wouldn't be able to read it. I was looking down the street when the dinner-bell rang.
Shoulder up, I reeled around to face Boo Radley and his bloody fangs; instead, I saw Dill ringing the bell with all his might in Atticus's face.
Jem looked so awful I didn't have the heart to tell him I told him so. He trudged along, dragging the pole behind him on the sidewalk.
Atticus said, "Stop ringing that bell."

Dill grabbed the clapper; in the silence that followed, I wished he'd start ringing it again. Atticus pushed his hat to the back of his head and put his hands on his hips. "Jem," he said, "what were you doing?"
"Nothin', sir."
"I don't want any of that. Tell me."
"I was—we were just tryin' to give somethin' to Mr. Radley."
"What were you trying to give him?"
"Just a letter."
"Let me see it."
Jem held out a filthy piece of paper. Atticus took it and tried to read it. "Why do you want Mr. Radley to come out?"
Dill said, "We thought he might enjoy us…" and dried up when Atticus looked at him.
"Son," he said to Jem, "I'm going to tell you something and tell you one time: stop tormenting that man. That goes for the other two of you."

What Mr. Radley did was his own business. If he wanted to come out, he would. If he wanted to stay inside his own house he had the right to stay inside free from the attentions of inquisitive children, which was a mild term for the likes of us. How would we like it if Atticus barged in on us without knocking, when we were in our rooms at night? We were, in effect, doing the same thing to Mr. Radley. What Mr. Radley did might seem peculiar to us, but it did not seem peculiar to him. Furthermore, had it never occurred to us that the civil way to communicate with another being was by the front door instead of a side window? Lastly, we were to stay away from that house until we were invited there, we were not to play an asinine game he had seen us playing or make fun of anybody on this street or in this town.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

"Can't get it off the pole," he muttered, "or if I get it off I can't make it stay. G'on back down the street, Scout."

I returned and gazed around the curve at the empty road. Occasionally I looked back at Jem, who was patiently trying to place the note on the window sill. It would flutter to the ground and Jem would jab it up, until I thought if Boo Radley ever received it he wouldn't be able to read it. I was looking down the street when the dinner-bell rang.

content.text: Jem's repeated jabbings with the fishing pole are intended to drop off the note at Boo Radley's window; they're not intended as a display of aggression.
Review the passage.

textContent.text: [Jem] scuttled beneath the house and came out with a yellow bamboo pole. "Reckon this is long enough to reach from the sidewalk?"
"Anybody who's brave enough to go up and touch the house hadn't oughta use a fishin' pole," I said. "Why don't you just knock the front door down?"
"This—is—different," said Jem, "how many times do I have to tell you that?"

Jem attached the note to the end of the fishing pole, let the pole out across the yard and pushed it toward the window he had selected. The pole lacked several inches of being long enough, and Jem leaned over as far as he could. I watched him making jabbing motions for so long, I abandoned my post and went to him.
"Can't get it off the pole," he muttered, "or if I get it off I can't make it stay. G'on back down the street, Scout."

I returned and gazed around the curve at the empty road. Occasionally I looked back at Jem, who was patiently trying to place the note on the window sill. It would flutter to the ground and Jem would jab it up, until I thought if Boo Radley ever received it he wouldn't be able to read it. I was looking down the street when the dinner-bell rang.
Shoulder up, I reeled around to face Boo Radley and his bloody fangs; instead, I saw Dill ringing the bell with all his might in Atticus's face.
Jem looked so awful I didn't have the heart to tell him I told him so. He trudged along, dragging the pole behind him on the sidewalk.
Atticus said, "Stop ringing that bell."

Dill grabbed the clapper; in the silence that followed, I wished he'd start ringing it again. Atticus pushed his hat to the back of his head and put his hands on his hips. "Jem," he said, "what were you doing?"
"Nothin', sir."
"I don't want any of that. Tell me."
"I was—we were just tryin' to give somethin' to Mr. Radley."
"What were you trying to give him?"
"Just a letter."
"Let me see it."
Jem held out a filthy piece of paper. Atticus took it and tried to read it. "Why do you want Mr. Radley to come out?"
Dill said, "We thought he might enjoy us…" and dried up when Atticus looked at him.
"Son," he said to Jem, "I'm going to tell you something and tell you one time: stop tormenting that man. That goes for the other two of you."

What Mr. Radley did was his own business. If he wanted to come out, he would. If he wanted to stay inside his own house he had the right to stay inside free from the attentions of inquisitive children, which was a mild term for the likes of us. How would we like it if Atticus barged in on us without knocking, when we were in our rooms at night? We were, in effect, doing the same thing to Mr. Radley. What Mr. Radley did might seem peculiar to us, but it did not seem peculiar to him. Furthermore, had it never occurred to us that the civil way to communicate with another being was by the front door instead of a side window? Lastly, we were to stay away from that house until we were invited there, we were not to play an asinine game he had seen us playing or make fun of anybody on this street or in this town.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

contents.text: The details in the passage suggest that this is Jem's strategy when an angry Atticus shows up:

text.text: He downplays the situation by asserting it is trivial.

content.text: Jem starts by telling Atticus that he wasn't doing anything. When pressed, he says they were "just" trying to give Mr. Radley a letter. His nonchalant language shows that he is trying to downplay their actions, making them seem trivial.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not suggest that these are Jem's strategy when Atticus shows up:

text.text: He argues with Atticus that their actions are harmless.

content.text: Though Jem initially tries to evade the question when Atticus asks what they are doing, he does not argue with Atticus, and he doesn't mention that their actions are harmless.

text.text: He lies about their intentions for delivering the note.

content.text: Jem first tries to say they were not doing anything, but when Atticus doesn't believe him, he quickly confesses about the note. He also does not attempt to explain their intentions.

text.text: He claims that Boo Radley would welcome their company.

content.text: It is Dill, not Jem, who says that they thought Boo Radley would enjoy their company.
Reread the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, Scout Finch, the narrator, is starting the first grade.

textContent.text: Miss Caroline began the day by reading us a story about cats. The cats had long conversations with one another, they wore cunning little clothes and lived in a warm house beneath a kitchen stove. By the time Mrs. Cat called the drugstore for an order of chocolate malted mice the class was wriggling like a bucketful of catawba worms. Miss Caroline seemed unaware that the ragged, denim-shirted and floursack-skirted first grade, most of whom had chopped cotton and fed hogs from the time they were able to walk, were immune to imaginative literature. Miss Caroline came to the end of the story and said, "Oh, my, wasn't that nice?"
Then she went to the blackboard and printed the alphabet in enormous square capitals, turned to the class and asked, "Does anybody know what these are?"
Everybody did; most of the first grade had failed it last year.

I suppose she chose me because she knew my name; as I read the alphabet a faint line appeared between her eyebrows, and after making me read most of My First Reader and the stock-market quotations from The Mobile Register aloud, she discovered that I was literate and looked at me with more than faint distaste. Miss Caroline told me to tell my father not to teach me any more, it would interfere with my reading.

"Teach me?" I said in surprise. "He hasn't taught me anything, Miss Caroline. Atticus ain't got time to teach me anything," I added, when Miss Caroline smiled and shook her head. "Why, he's so tired at night he just sits in the living room and reads."

"If he didn't teach you, who did?" Miss Caroline asked good-naturedly. "Somebody did. You weren't born reading The Mobile Register […] Now you tell your father not to teach you any more. It's best to begin reading with a fresh mind. You tell him I'll take over from here and try to undo the damage—"
"Ma'am?"
"Your father does not know how to teach. You can have a seat now."

I mumbled that I was sorry and retired meditating upon my crime. I never deliberately learned to read, but somehow I had been wallowing illicitly in the daily papers. In the long hours of church—was it then I learned? I could not remember not being able to read hymns. Now that I was compelled to think about it, reading was something that just came to me, as learning to fasten the seat of my union suit without looking around, or achieving two bows from a snarl of shoelaces. I could not remember when the lines above Atticus's moving finger separated into words, but I had stared at them all the evenings in my memory, listening to the news of the day, Bills To Be Enacted into Laws, the diaries of Lorenzo Dow—anything Atticus happened to be reading when I crawled into his lap every night. Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

By the time Mrs. Cat called the drugstore for an order of chocolate malted mice the class was wriggling like a bucketful of catawba worms. Miss Caroline seemed unaware that the ragged, denim-shirted and floursack-skirted first grade, most of whom had chopped cotton and fed hogs from the time they were able to walk, were immune to imaginative literature. Miss Caroline came to the end of the story and said, "Oh, my, wasn't that nice?"
Then she went to the blackboard and printed the alphabet in enormous square capitals, turned to the class and asked, "Does anybody know what these are?"
Everybody did; most of the first grade had failed it last year.

I suppose she chose me because she knew my name; as I read the alphabet a faint line appeared between her eyebrows, and after making me read most of My First Reader and the stock-market quotations from The Mobile Register aloud, she discovered that I was literate and looked at me with more than faint distaste. Miss Caroline told me to tell my father not to teach me any more, it would interfere with my reading.

"Teach me?" I said in surprise. "He hasn't taught me anything, Miss Caroline. Atticus ain't got time to teach me anything," I added, when Miss Caroline smiled and shook her head. "Why, he's so tired at night he just sits in the living room and reads."

"If he didn't teach you, who did?" Miss Caroline asked good-naturedly. "Somebody did. You weren't born reading The Mobile Register […] Now you tell your father not to teach you any more. It's best to begin reading with a fresh mind. You tell him I'll take over from here and try to undo the damage—"
"Ma'am?"
"Your father does not know how to teach. You can have a seat now."

I mumbled that I was sorry and retired meditating upon my crime. I never deliberately learned to read, but somehow I had been wallowing illicitly in the daily papers. In the long hours of church—was it then I learned? I could not remember not being able to read hymns. Now that I was compelled to think about it, reading was something that just came to me, as learning to fasten the seat of my union suit without looking around, or achieving two bows from a snarl of shoelaces. I could not remember when the lines above Atticus's moving finger separated into words, but I had stared at them all the evenings in my memory, listening to the news of the day, Bills To Be Enacted into Laws, the diaries of Lorenzo Dow—anything Atticus happened to be reading when I crawled into his lap every night. Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

contents.text: The details in the passage support this inference about Scout's relationship with reading prior to her conversation with Miss Caroline:

text.text: It was something she did naturally and did not give much thought to.

content.text: Up until this point, Scout has never considered when exactly she learned to read and reflects, "reading was something that just came to me." She compares reading to breathing, another activity that people do naturally and thus do not give much thought to.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not support these inferences about Scout's relationship with reading:

text.text: It was a hobby she passionately pursued and eagerly looked forward to doing.

content.text: Scout reflects, "Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read," revealing that she did not have a passion for reading prior to her conversation with Miss Caroline.

text.text: It was a skill that gave her great pride because it came so easily to her.

content.text: Scout does not show particular pride in her ability to read. She only reads in front of the class because her teacher asks her to, and she compares the act of reading to mundane activities like putting on clothes or tying shoes.

text.text: It was something forbidden that she practiced in secret.

content.text: Scout reads by sitting with her father and following along with the words he is reading, so it is not something she had perceived as forbidden or practiced in secret.

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird
tells the story of Scout Finch, a young girl growing up in a small town in Alabama in the 1930s, during a period of widespread racial segregation in the United States.

pieces.text: At the beginning of the novel, Scout and her brother, Jem, keep themselves busy by plotting to uncover the mysteries of their reclusive neighbor, Mr. Arthur "Boo" Radley. But when their father, well-respected lawyer Atticus Finch, sparks controversy by agreeing to defend an African American man in an upcoming trial, Scout's world turns upside-down.

content.text: Scout and her family are forced to reckon with the hate and racial prejudice embedded in their community.

pieces.text: When it was first published in 1960,

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: resonated with countless readers experiencing the turmoil of the Civil Rights Movement in the United States. The novel is famous for the way it uses the innocent perspective of a child to illuminate the brutal realities of racism in the United States during that period of American history.

Miss Caroline seemed unaware that the ragged, denim-shirted and floursack-skirted first grade, most of whom had chopped cotton and fed hogs from the time they were able to walk, were immune to imaginative literature. Miss Caroline came to the end of the story and said, "Oh, my, wasn't that nice?"
Then she went to the blackboard and printed the alphabet in enormous square capitals, turned to the class and asked, "Does anybody know what these are?"
Everybody did; most of the first grade had failed it last year.

I suppose she chose me because she knew my name; as I read the alphabet a faint line appeared between her eyebrows, and after making me read most of My First Reader and the stock-market quotations from The Mobile Register aloud, she discovered that I was literate and looked at me with more than faint distaste. Miss Caroline told me to tell my father not to teach me any more, it would interfere with my reading.

"Teach me?" I said in surprise. "He hasn't taught me anything, Miss Caroline. Atticus ain't got time to teach me anything," I added, when Miss Caroline smiled and shook her head. "Why, he's so tired at night he just sits in the living room and reads."

"If he didn't teach you, who did?" Miss Caroline asked good-naturedly. "Somebody did. You weren't born reading The Mobile Register […] Now you tell your father not to teach you any more. It's best to begin reading with a fresh mind. You tell him I'll take over from here and try to undo the damage—"
"Ma'am?"
"Your father does not know how to teach. You can have a seat now."

I mumbled that I was sorry and retired meditating upon my crime. I never deliberately learned to read, but somehow I had been wallowing illicitly in the daily papers. In the long hours of church—was it then I learned? I could not remember not being able to read hymns. Now that I was compelled to think about it, reading was something that just came to me, as learning to fasten the seat of my union suit without looking around, or achieving two bows from a snarl of shoelaces. I could not remember when the lines above Atticus's moving finger separated into words, but I had stared at them all the evenings in my memory, listening to the news of the day, Bills To Be Enacted into Laws, the diaries of Lorenzo Dow—anything Atticus happened to be reading when I crawled into his lap every night. Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.

So, this line is used to illustrate how people often take for granted abilities that they exercise frequently and naturally.

content.text: Read the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, Scout Finch (the narrator), Jem (her brother), and Dill (a friend) attempt to deliver a note to Mr. Arthur "Boo" Radley, their mysterious and reclusive neighbor, before they are caught by Atticus (Scout and Jem's father).

textContent.text: [Jem] scuttled beneath the house and came out with a yellow bamboo pole. "Reckon this is long enough to reach from the sidewalk?"
"Anybody who's brave enough to go up and touch the house hadn't oughta use a fishin' pole," I said. "Why don't you just knock the front door down?"
"This—is—different," said Jem, "how many times do I have to tell you that?"

Jem attached the note to the end of the fishing pole, let the pole out across the yard and pushed it toward the window he had selected. The pole lacked several inches of being long enough, and Jem leaned over as far as he could. I watched him making jabbing motions for so long, I abandoned my post and went to him.
"Can't get it off the pole," he muttered, "or if I get it off I can't make it stay. G'on back down the street, Scout."

I returned and gazed around the curve at the empty road. Occasionally I looked back at Jem, who was patiently trying to place the note on the window sill. It would flutter to the ground and Jem would jab it up, until I thought if Boo Radley ever received it he wouldn't be able to read it. I was looking down the street when the dinner-bell rang.
Shoulder up, I reeled around to face Boo Radley and his bloody fangs; instead, I saw Dill ringing the bell with all his might in Atticus's face.
Jem looked so awful I didn't have the heart to tell him I told him so. He trudged along, dragging the pole behind him on the sidewalk.
Atticus said, "Stop ringing that bell."

Dill grabbed the clapper; in the silence that followed, I wished he'd start ringing it again. Atticus pushed his hat to the back of his head and put his hands on his hips. "Jem," he said, "what were you doing?"
"Nothin', sir."
"I don't want any of that. Tell me."
"I was—we were just tryin' to give somethin' to Mr. Radley."
"What were you trying to give him?"
"Just a letter."
"Let me see it."
Jem held out a filthy piece of paper. Atticus took it and tried to read it. "Why do you want Mr. Radley to come out?"
Dill said, "We thought he might enjoy us…" and dried up when Atticus looked at him.
"Son," he said to Jem, "I'm going to tell you something and tell you one time: stop tormenting that man. That goes for the other two of you."

What Mr. Radley did was his own business. If he wanted to come out, he would. If he wanted to stay inside his own house he had the right to stay inside free from the attentions of inquisitive children, which was a mild term for the likes of us. How would we like it if Atticus barged in on us without knocking, when we were in our rooms at night? We were, in effect, doing the same thing to Mr. Radley. What Mr. Radley did might seem peculiar to us, but it did not seem peculiar to him. Furthermore, had it never occurred to us that the civil way to communicate with another being was by the front door instead of a side window? Lastly, we were to stay away from that house until we were invited there, we were not to play an asinine game he had seen us playing or make fun of anybody on this street or in this town.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

text.text: "This—is—different," said Jem, "how many times do I have to tell you that?"

content.text: When Scout asks Jem why he doesn't just knock on the front door, Jem stammers that the situation is different, but he doesn't give any further reason. This implies that Jem feels uncomfortable with the possibility of directly confronting Boo Radley.

text.text: Shoulder up, I reeled around to face Boo Radley and his bloody fangs; instead, I saw Dill ringing the bell with all his might in Atticus's face.

content.text: When Scout hears the bell ringing, she turns around in a panic expecting to see Boo Radley behind her and imagines him with "bloody fangs." This gory image shows that Scout is frightened at the possibility of being face-to-face with Boo Radley.

textContent.text: [Jem] scuttled beneath the house and came out with a yellow bamboo pole. "Reckon this is long enough to reach from the sidewalk?"
"Anybody who's brave enough to go up and touch the house hadn't oughta use a fishin' pole," I said. "Why don't you just knock the front door down?"
"This—is—different," said Jem, "how many times do I have to tell you that?"

Jem attached the note to the end of the fishing pole, let the pole out across the yard and pushed it toward the window he had selected. The pole lacked several inches of being long enough, and Jem leaned over as far as he could. I watched him making jabbing motions for so long, I abandoned my post and went to him.
"Can't get it off the pole," he muttered, "or if I get it off I can't make it stay. G'on back down the street, Scout."

I returned and gazed around the curve at the empty road. Occasionally I looked back at Jem, who was patiently trying to place the note on the window sill. It would flutter to the ground and Jem would jab it up, until I thought if Boo Radley ever received it he wouldn't be able to read it. I was looking down the street when the dinner-bell rang.
Shoulder up, I reeled around to face Boo Radley and his bloody fangs; instead, I saw Dill ringing the bell with all his might in Atticus's face.
Jem looked so awful I didn't have the heart to tell him I told him so. He trudged along, dragging the pole behind him on the sidewalk.
Atticus said, "Stop ringing that bell."

Dill grabbed the clapper; in the silence that followed, I wished he'd start ringing it again. Atticus pushed his hat to the back of his head and put his hands on his hips. "Jem," he said, "what were you doing?"
"Nothin', sir."
"I don't want any of that. Tell me."
"I was—we were just tryin' to give somethin' to Mr. Radley."
"What were you trying to give him?"
"Just a letter."
"Let me see it."
Jem held out a filthy piece of paper. Atticus took it and tried to read it. "Why do you want Mr. Radley to come out?"
Dill said, "We thought he might enjoy us…" and dried up when Atticus looked at him.
"Son," he said to Jem, "I'm going to tell you something and tell you one time: stop tormenting that man. That goes for the other two of you."

What Mr. Radley did was his own business. If he wanted to come out, he would. If he wanted to stay inside his own house he had the right to stay inside free from the attentions of inquisitive children, which was a mild term for the likes of us. How would we like it if Atticus barged in on us without knocking, when we were in our rooms at night? We were, in effect, doing the same thing to Mr. Radley. What Mr. Radley did might seem peculiar to us, but it did not seem peculiar to him. Furthermore, had it never occurred to us that the civil way to communicate with another being was by the front door instead of a side window? Lastly, we were to stay away from that house until we were invited there, we were not to play an asinine game he had seen us playing or make fun of anybody on this street or in this town.

content.text: Reread the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, Scout Finch, the narrator, is starting the first grade.

textContent.text: Miss Caroline began the day by reading us a story about cats. The cats had long conversations with one another, they wore cunning little clothes and lived in a warm house beneath a kitchen stove. By the time Mrs. Cat called the drugstore for an order of chocolate malted mice the class was wriggling like a bucketful of catawba worms. Miss Caroline seemed unaware that the ragged, denim-shirted and floursack-skirted first grade, most of whom had chopped cotton and fed hogs from the time they were able to walk, were immune to imaginative literature. Miss Caroline came to the end of the story and said, "Oh, my, wasn't that nice?"
Then she went to the blackboard and printed the alphabet in enormous square capitals, turned to the class and asked, "Does anybody know what these are?"
Everybody did; most of the first grade had failed it last year.

I suppose she chose me because she knew my name; as I read the alphabet a faint line appeared between her eyebrows, and after making me read most of My First Reader and the stock-market quotations from The Mobile Register aloud, she discovered that I was literate and looked at me with more than faint distaste. Miss Caroline told me to tell my father not to teach me any more, it would interfere with my reading.

"Teach me?" I said in surprise. "He hasn't taught me anything, Miss Caroline. Atticus ain't got time to teach me anything," I added, when Miss Caroline smiled and shook her head. "Why, he's so tired at night he just sits in the living room and reads."

"If he didn't teach you, who did?" Miss Caroline asked good-naturedly. "Somebody did. You weren't born reading The Mobile Register […] Now you tell your father not to teach you any more. It's best to begin reading with a fresh mind. You tell him I'll take over from here and try to undo the damage—"
"Ma'am?"
"Your father does not know how to teach. You can have a seat now."

I mumbled that I was sorry and retired meditating upon my crime. I never deliberately learned to read, but somehow I had been wallowing illicitly in the daily papers. In the long hours of church—was it then I learned? I could not remember not being able to read hymns. Now that I was compelled to think about it, reading was something that just came to me, as learning to fasten the seat of my union suit without looking around, or achieving two bows from a snarl of shoelaces. I could not remember when the lines above Atticus's moving finger separated into words, but I had stared at them all the evenings in my memory, listening to the news of the day, Bills To Be Enacted into Laws, the diaries of Lorenzo Dow—anything Atticus happened to be reading when I crawled into his lap every night. Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.
From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee

contents.text: Argumentative writing is based on claims, evidence, and analysis. Analysis explains how and why the evidence supports the claim.
Strong analysis makes this connection by providing a statement of value, underlying principle, or general interpretive rule that helps readers to understand how the evidence supports the claim.

header.text: A statement of value is a statement about fundamental priorities that can be used to guide decisions.

sentences.text: Claim: Parents should not let their children watch television for more than an hour per day.
Evidence: Children who watch several hours of television per day spend less time outside than they would otherwise.
Analysis: It's vital that children spend time outside.

header.text: An underlying principle is a belief or understanding about how the world works.

sentences.text: Claim: Romeo and Juliet do not really love each other.
Evidence: They claim to be in love after only a few brief conversations.
Analysis: True love requires long periods of time in which two people get to know each other.

header.text: A general interpretive rule is a rule that can be used to interpret a certain type of information.

contents.text: A relative pronoun introduces a relative clause that describes a noun or pronoun.
The relative pronouns who and whom give information about people.

header.text: To figure out whether to use who or whom, restate the relative clause with a personal pronoun. If the clause uses a subject pronoun (he, she, or they), use who. If the clause uses an object pronoun (him, her, or them), use whom.

contents.text: A relative pronoun introduces a relative clause that describes a noun or pronoun. The five main relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that.
The relative pronouns who and whom give information about people.

header.text: To figure out whether to use who or whom, restate the relative clause with a personal pronoun. If the clause uses a subject pronoun (he, she, or they), use who. If the clause uses an object pronoun (him, her, or them), use whom.

sentences.text: The woman who lives next door grows tomatoes in her garden.
She lives next door.
Peter, whom you met yesterday, has four younger brothers.
You met him yesterday.

header.text: The relative pronoun that gives necessary information about things. Necessary information narrows down what you're talking about and is not set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to a park that has a tire swing.
The information narrows down which park we walked to. It is necessary.

header.text: The relative pronoun which adds unnecessary information about things. This extra information does not narrow down what you're talking about. It is always set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to Glendale Park, which has a tire swing.
The information is extra. It does not narrow down which park we walked to.

header.text: The relative pronoun whose shows possession.

contents.text: Emily, whose hair is quite long, likes wearing braids.

header.text: Do not confuse whose with who's. Who's is a contraction for who is or who has. It does not show possession.

sentences.text: Emily, who's quite tall, can reach the top shelf.
Emily, who is quite tall, can reach the top shelf.
